A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work, retaining the decentralized learning problem, spectral attack, and substantial theoretical material. All 22 pages of v1 and 24 pages of v2, including figures and appendices, support comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original MNIST classification experiments comparing aggregation methods under four Byzantine attacks in Figure 1.

after.justification: v2 reports original MNIST, CIFAR-10, and synthetic averaging experiments in Figures 1–4 and Appendix B.

M1.justification: v1's CG+ uses the stated (b+1)-st largest neighbor difference as its clipping threshold. v2 introduces weighted F–RG and CSours with a tail-weight threshold of 2b, corresponding to the 2b-th largest difference for unit weights. It also introduces oracle clipping and an asynchronous adaptation (Sections 3–4).

E1.justification: v1 evaluates MNIST classification only. v2 retains MNIST and adds CIFAR-10 classification and synthetic five-dimensional approximate averaging (Appendices B.2–B.3), substantially extending dataset and task coverage. The four attack types and honest graph topology are retained.

E2.justification: The trimming comparator MoNNA/NNA and adaptive ClippedGossip correspond to GTS–RG and CSHe–RG in v2's unit-weight experiments. However, the unattacked D-SGD reference in v1's MNIST Figure 1 is absent from v2's MNIST Figures 1–2; it appears in the new CIFAR-10 comparison instead.

E3.justification: v1 Figure 1 shows MNIST accuracy trajectories through 200 iterations at b=6. v2 Figures 1–2 measure loss and accuracy after 300 steps over b=1–10. Added protocols include CIFAR-10 training for 2000 iterations at b=5 and communication-only averaging evaluated by relative MSE after 100 steps.

E4.justification: v1 compares four attacks at one corruption level. v2 adds corruption-level sweeps that examine where methods break down, plus controlled averaging experiments that isolate communication behavior from model training (Figures 1, 2, and 4). These substantially expand robustness and sensitivity analysis.

E5.justification: v1 Figure 1 contains shaded bands without explaining their meaning or reporting run counts. v2 specifies five MNIST seeds and ten averaging initializations, reporting means and minimum–maximum ranges, and discloses that CIFAR-10 uses one seed. This clarifies statistical reporting without establishing an increase from a known v1 run count.

E6.justification: The fixed-corruption MNIST trajectories are replaced by loss and accuracy results across corruption levels. New CIFAR-10 results show GTS–RG failing under SpH while CSours–RG and CSHe–RG fail under FOE (Figure 3); Figure 4 adds averaging-error results. These are new or replaced results under changed conditions, not demonstrated same-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: v2 introduces weighted graph definitions, (b,rho)-robust summation, general convergence results, and oracle/asynchronous guarantees. The practical guarantee changes from 2(b+1)<mu_min to 4b<mu_min, with revised clipping proofs in Appendix E. The lower bound is generalized to weighted neighborhoods. However, v2's Clipped Sum definition includes a 1/n normalization absent from its Appendix E.1 analysis.

C1.justification: v1 centers its contributions on a practical CG+ algorithm attaining optimal breakdown up to an additive constant. v2 centers a unifying F–RG framework and claims near-optimal practical breakdown. Exact optimality is assigned to an oracle rule, while practical attainment remains open (abstract, introduction, and Section 3.4).

C2.justification: v2 explicitly identifies the unresolved practical/oracle optimality gap and attributes it to threshold selection (Sections 3.4–4.1). It adds an explanation of why aggregating parameter differences handles heterogeneity and interprets low-heterogeneity MNIST results as exposing connectivity limitations. These materially qualify and expand v1's interpretation.

D1.justification: v2 documents the per-node attack-search objective, unit edge weights, CIFAR-10 architecture and learning rate, and synthetic initialization procedure. Conversely, it removes v1's explicit project-code link and MNIST CNN architecture description. The expanded attack-search description alone does not establish that the underlying search procedure changed.

R1.justification: Positioning shifts from an improved hybrid of NNA and ClippedGossip to a framework encompassing these and other robust aggregators. v2 adds the concurrent ARC comparison and Pillutla et al. (2022), while removing several contextual references. The changed dates for ClippedGossip and bucketing identify the same works, rather than new citations.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, contributions, and methodological narrative are extensively rewritten around the general framework. The lower bound moves into Section 3.4, attack-centering details move to Appendix A, and the former proof appendix is reorganized into Appendices C–F alongside a new experimental appendix. This exceeds terminology or numbering changes.

P2.justification: The main text changes from single-column to two-column layout. v1's theoretical comparison table disappears; its MNIST learning-curve display is replaced by corruption-sweep plots. CIFAR-10 and averaging figures are added, and the lower-bound topology illustration is redrawn and relocated as Figure 5.

improvement.justification: Replacing v1's invalid clipping-error argument in Lemma 7 and practical-optimality claim with a revised threshold, analysis, and explicit practical/oracle gap substantially improves scientific reliability. Corruption sweeps and isolated averaging tests directly examine breakdown, while CIFAR-10 exposes failures of the proposed method. These gains outweigh the removed code link and unresolved normalization/sign inconsistencies between v2's main definitions and appendices.
